args.text: [lane-ibis] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to an old server after a site moves or fails over, so they see errors or outages. (2) Slow security fixes: if a record is poisoned or a domain is hijacked, the bad answer lingers until the cache expires. (3) Delayed change rollout: planned moves, certificate changes or traffic shifts take far longer to reach everyone, and the exact delay is unknown.

[lane-ibis] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave you unsure whether a request worked, so you must be able to send it again. If the request is idempotent (repeating it gives the same result as doing it once), a retry cannot cause harm such as a double payment or a duplicate order.

[lane-ibis] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (a universally unique identifier whose first part is a timestamp) as a primary key: (1) Good: because the values rise roughly with time, new rows land near each other in the index, so inserts are faster and pages fragment less than with random UUIDs. (2) Bad: each key is 16 bytes, larger than a typical 8-byte integer, and the embedded timestamp leaks when a row was created, which may matter for privacy or guessing patterns.

[lane-ibis] A write-ahead log is a record of every change that a database writes to disc before it applies that change to the main data files. If the system crashes part-way through, it can replay the log on restart to recover completed work and undo unfinished work, so no data is lost or left half-written.

[lane-ibis] (1) Pinning the client version keeps results comparable: if the client changes between runs, any speed difference might come from the client rather than the system under test. (2) It makes the benchmark repeatable, so others can rerun the exact setup later and get the same behaviour, without hidden changes to defaults, retries or connection handling.

[lane-ibis] Backpressure is the way a queue tells producers to slow down or stop when consumers cannot keep up, for example by refusing new items, making senders wait, or signalling that the queue is nearly full. This stops the queue growing without limit, which would otherwise use up memory and make delays worse for everyone.

[lane-ibis] Two ways a cron job can run twice: (1) the same schedule is set up on two machines, or a deployment leaves a duplicate entry; (2) a run takes longer than the interval, so the next run starts while the first is still going. One guard: take a lock (for example a lock file or a database lock) at the start, and exit at once if another run already holds it.

[lane-ibis] A tombstone is a marker saved in place of a deleted item, so that every copy of the data learns the item was removed. Without it, a copy that missed the delete could send the old value back and bring the item to life again; tombstones are kept for a set time and then cleared.

[lane-ibis] Two signs a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code with no change, so a re-run gives a different result; (2) the failures depend on things like timing, test order or shared state, so they appear only now and then or only on some machines.

[lane-ibis] A lease lock gives a holder the lock only until a set time, and each machine judges that time by its own clock. If the holder's clock runs slow compared with the lock service's clock, it believes it still holds the lease after the service has given it to someone else, so two holders act at once. A pause in the holder, such as a long garbage-collection stop, causes the same fault; fencing tokens (a rising number checked by the store) guard against it.
